newsitem.title: INDIA: Bombay shares end higher on political hopes.
newsitem.headline: Bombay shares end higher on political hopes.

text.p: Bombay shares ended sharply above early lows on Friday as leaders of the ruling United Front and Congress Party met in a bid to defuse a political crisis.
"The knee jerk reaction was swift and upwards," said Ketan Jhaveri, chief dealer at Kotak Securities, the Indian partner of Goldman Sachs & Co.
Leaders of the UF and Congress said they were searching for a successor to Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda, in a deal which could stop the country plunging headlong into mid-term polls.
Comments from the Finance Minister P. Chidambaram's voicing confidence on the budget for 1997/98 also perked sentiment.
"The key issue for the market is whether the budget will be passed. It's almost become an independent issue," said Rupa Bose, strategist at Paribas Capital Markets in Singapore.
Leaders of both political parties said a consensus candidate for the top job could be named by the UF before a vote of confidence scheduled for later on Friday, or soon afterwards.
"We are expecting a change in leadership," Hannan Mollah, a deputy of the Communist Party of India-Marxist, told Reuters after Deve Gowda moved the motion of confidence in parliament.
Share prices skidded in early trade as it appeared that the government faced almost certain defeat in the trust vote.
"If the parties reach a consensus it will be very good for the market," Kotak's Jhaveri said.
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram in the budget unveiled on February 28 announced sweeping cuts in corporate and personal taxes, leading to a sharp rally in share prices.

"I am still hopeful that all political parties will find some way in which parliament can discharge its responsibility of passing the Finance Bill," Chidambaram told reporters during a break in parliamentary debate on Friday.
